title: Body & health
goal: Name parts of the body, say what's wrong when you're ill, understand a doctor's advice and give simple advice yourself.
intro:
When you're ill in Nepali, illnesses *come to you* or *strike you*: **मलाई ज्वरो आयो** 'a fever came to me', **मलाई रुघा लाग्यो** 'a cold struck me'. A part of your body *hurts by itself*: **मेरो टाउको दुख्यो** 'my head hurt'. This builds on the मलाई construction from unit 5.

You'll also learn to say what someone **should** or **shouldn't** do — handy for following a doctor's or a pharmacist's instructions.

vocab.note: मलाई ज्वरो आयो 'I have a fever'.
The body part is the subject: मेरो दाँत दुख्छ 'my tooth hurts'.

vocab.en: to strike, affect; to feel; to seem; to start
vocab.note: One of the most useful verbs: भोक लाग्यो, रुघा लाग्यो, चोट लाग्यो, राम्रो लाग्यो 'I liked it/it seemed good'.
औषधि खानु 'to take medicine' (lit. eat). Pharmacy: औषधि पसल.
मलाई पखाला लाग्यो. Common for new arrivals!

phrases.en: What's wrong? (lit. what happened to you?)
Please take me to a doctor.

phrases.native: यो औषधि दिनको तीन पटक खानुहोस्।
phrases.roman: yo ausadhi dinko tin paṭak khānuhos.
phrases.en: Take this medicine three times a day.

grammar.title: Saying what's wrong
grammar.body:
Nepali describes illness as something that happens **to** you. Three patterns cover almost everything:

**1. मलाई + illness + आयो / लाग्यो** — 'X came / struck to me':
मलाई ज्वरो **आयो** (fever) · मलाई रुघा **लाग्यो** (cold) · खोकी लाग्यो (cough) · पखाला लाग्यो (diarrhoea) · वाकवाकी लाग्यो (nausea) · चोट लाग्यो (injury).

**2. मेरो + body part + दुख्यो / दुख्छ** — 'my X hurts': मेरो टाउको दुख्यो 'I have a headache', मेरो दाँत दुख्छ 'my tooth hurts'. Use the progressive दुखिरहेको छ for 'is hurting right now'.

**3. म बिरामी छु** — 'I am ill', or **मलाई सन्चो छैन** 'I'm not well'.

The doctor's question is **के भयो?** 'What happened?' or **के समस्या छ?** 'What's the problem?'.

examples.en: She has a cold and a cough.

grammar.title: 'Should' and 'shouldn't'
grammar.body:
**-नुपर्छ** (verb stem + नु + पर्छ, lit. 'it falls to do') means 'must / need to / should': **आराम गर्नुपर्छ** 'you should rest'. The doer can take **-ले**: तपाईंले… (unit 16 explains ले fully) or **-लाई**: तपाईंलाई अस्पताल जानुपर्छ.

**-नुहुँदैन** means 'must not / shouldn't' (lit. 'it doesn't do to'): चिसो पानी **खानुहुँदैन** 'you shouldn't drink cold water'.

A gentler suggestion: **[verb]-ए हुन्छ** 'it'd be fine to / you could': औषधि खाए हुन्छ 'you could take some medicine'. And **-नु राम्रो** 'it's better to'.

examples.en: You should drink lots of water.
I need to go to the doctor.
You shouldn't go to work when you're ill.
You could take a rest today.
It's better to get a check-up in the morning.

dialogue.title: At the clinic
dialogue.setting: Tom feels ill after eating street food and goes to a small clinic in Thamel.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: Please sit down. What's the matter?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: हिजो रातिदेखि मलाई ज्वरो आएको छ।
lines.roman: hijo rātidekhi malāi jwaro āeko chha.
lines.en: I've had a fever since last night.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: टाउको दुख्छ, अनि पेट पनि दुख्छ।
lines.roman: ṭāuko dukhchha, ani peṭ pani dukhchha.
lines.en: My head aches, and my stomach hurts too.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: A little. I feel nauseous too.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: I had panipuri on the street.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: त्यसैले होला। यो औषधि दिनको दुई पटक खानुहोस्, र उमालेको पानी मात्र खानुहोस्।
lines.roman: tyasaile holā. yo ausadhi dinko dui paṭak khānuhos, ra umāleko pāni mātra khānuhos.
lines.en: That'll be why. Take this medicine twice a day, and drink only boiled water.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: You need to rest for two days.

culture: In the mountains, altitude sickness is called **लेक लाग्नु** *lek lāgnu* 'the high hills strike you' — guides will tell you बिस्तारै, बिस्तारै 'slowly, slowly' and to drink lots of water and garlic soup. Many medicines can be bought over the counter at an **औषधि पसल**, and the pharmacist often acts as a first doctor. Alongside modern medicine, many Nepalis also use Ayurveda, home remedies (hot water, turmeric, ginger) and, in villages, traditional healers (**धामी-झाँक्री**).
